Abstract
Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit im-
pressive capabilities but also present risks such
as biased content generation and privacy issues.
One of the current alignment techniques in-
cludes principle-driven integration, but it faces
challenges arising from the imprecision of man-
ually crafted rules and inadequate risk percep-
tion in models without safety training. To ad-
dress these, we introduce Guide-Align, a two-
stage approach. Initially, a safety-trained model
identifies potential risks and formulates spe-
cific guidelines for various inputs, establish
ing a comprehensive library of guidelines and
a model for input-guidelines retrieval. Sub
sequently, the retrieval model correlates new
inputs with relevant guidelines, which guide
LLMs in response generation to ensure safe
and high-quality outputs, thereby aligning with
human values. An additional optional stage in
volves fine-tuning a model with well-aligned
datasets generated through the process imple-
mented in the second stage. Our method cus
tomizes guidelines to accommodate diverse in-
puts, thereby enhancing the fine-grainedness
and comprehensiveness of the guideline li
brary. Furthermore, it incorporates safety ex-
pertise from a safety-trained LLM through a
lightweight retrieval model. We evaluate our
approach on three benchmarks, demonstrat-
ing significant improvements in LLM security
and quality. Notably, our fine-tuned model,
Labrador, even at 13 billion parameters, out-
performs GPT-3.5-turbo and surpasses GPT-4
in alignment capabilities.<sup>1</sup>

quently, they offer less precise guidance than those
tailored for nuanced, fine-grained matching. b.

Insufficient Risk Perception Models without
safety training often lack risk perception, making
them ineffective at identifying insecure information
within a context. As a result, they are more likely
to generate insecure outputs from diverse inputs.
Current research approaches, whether they involve
prompting AI for self-critique and revision(Bai
et al., 2022b) or enabling the model to select and
adhere to rules(Sun et al., 2023b), rely on a basic
level of security risk awareness of the model. How-
ever, models without safety training face challenges
in performing these tasks autonomously, particu-
larly without external aids like in-context learning
examples.
To address the above issues, we propose a novel
method called Guide-Align. This approach au-
tonomously generates a comprehensive library of
detailed guidelines tailored to diverse inputs. We
also train a retrieval model to associate inputs with
relevant guidelines. These resources are then used
to guide LLMs during response generation, ensur-
ing safe and high-quality outputs, thereby aligning
with human values. As an optional step, we apply
our method to open-source input data, creating an
alignment dataset. This dataset is used to fine-tune
a large model, which we call Labrador.
We foster a more fine-grained match between
inputs and guidelines by tailoring specific guide-
lines for each input. Additionally, we enhance the
comprehensiveness of the guideline repository by
introducing diversity in inputs while constructing
the guideline library. These dual strategies enable
our method to overcome limitations associated with
manually written rules.
Furthermore, we address the safety awareness
deficit in the model lacking safety training by inte-
grating the security expertise derived from a more
robust, safety-trained LLM through a lightweight
retrieval model.
In summary, our contributions are as follows:
• We introduce a novel method named Guide-
Align for aligning models with human values.
• We provide a plug-and-play component with a
comprehensive and detailed guideline library
and a corresponding retrieval model. This
component markedly augments the security
and quality of LLMs.
• We construct an alignment dataset to pro-
vide a valuable resource to facilitate the align-
ment of models with human values. Fur-
thermore, we utilize this dataset to train a
model named Labrador. Despite a parameter
scale of 13 billion, Labrador exhibits per-
formance that surpasses GPT-3.5-turbo and
exceeds the alignment capabilities of GPT-4
on three benchmarks.

phases: Guideline Library Construction and Re-

2.1 Guideline Library Construction and
Retrieval Model Training
In this phase, a safety-trained LLM meticulously
analyzes the input data from the training set, deter-
mining whether it contains unsafe content or has
the potential to prompt AI assistants to generate
insecure or inappropriate responses. This step aims
to enable the safety-trained LLM to develop tar-
geted rules for safety-relevant input data.
In the event of an affirmative determination by
the model (indicated by the term "yes" in the re-
sponse), the model, contextualizing the safety de-
tection step, is then instructed to formulate guide-
lines. These guidelines serve to direct AI assis-
tants, ensuring the safety of their responses when
confronted with such inputs. Conversely, if the
model determines that the input is devoid of inse-
cure content (i.e., indicated by the term "no" in the
response), the model is instructed to generate guide-
lines to enhance the overall quality of AI assistants’
responses when presented with such inputs, with-
out considering the context generated by the safety
detection step. An illustrative example of a safety-
related input and its corresponding set of guidelines

2.2 Inference
During the inference stage, the trained retrieval
model extracts relevant guidelines from the guide-
line library for each given input. Given that guide-
lines are tailored to specific inputs, an influx of in-
put data may result in numerous similar guidelines
within the library. To ensure precision in matching,
we selectively clean nearly identical guidelines, re-
fraining from stringent deduplication. As a result,
the retrieved guidelines may still exhibit substan-
tial similarity. Subsequently, we employ a process
based on string fuzzy matching on the retrieved
guideline set to impose a more stringent elimina-
tion of duplications. The resultant top-k guidelines,
post-deduplication, are concatenated with the orig-
inal input and presented to the LLM to generate
safe and high-quality responses.
2.3 Fine-tuning (Optional)
Furthermore, we introduce an optional fine-tuning
phase. Consistent with the workflow employed
during the inference stage, we leverage instruc-
tions from an open-source dataset to generate well-
aligned responses. However, there is a divergence
from the inference stage: to enhance the quality
of the generated dataset, we incorporate a small
number of examples to assist the model in better
adhering to the guidelines. Significantly, these ex-
amples are not utilized during the inference stage.
The generated responses, in conjunction with the
instructions, constitute our newly formed dataset.
Subsequently, we utilize this dataset to fine-tune a
base model, resulting in a refined model, termed
Labrador, which is characterized by its alignment
with human values.
3 Experiment
3.1 Experiment Setup
During the construction of the guideline library, a
temperature value of 0.7 is applied to the safety-
trained model (referred to as GPT-3.5-turbo in our
paper). Throughout the inference and fine-tuning
stages, LLMs are decoded with a temperature of 0
to minimize the randomness. We initially retrieve
20 guidelines for each input, and subsequently sam-
ple the top 6 after removing duplicates. The dedu-
plication threshold is defined at 0.53. Further de-
tails regarding the experimental setup are provided
in Section E.
3.2 The Statistic Information of Training Set
And Guideline Library
During the construction of the guideline library and
the training of the retrieval model, we formulate
guidelines encompassing 52k security-independent
questions drawn from Self-instruct (Wang et al.,
2023a) and 100k security-related questions devel-
oped following the methodology proposed by Sun
et al. (2023a). This aggregation yields a cumula-
tive total of 767k guidelines, and detailed statisti-
cal information can be found in Table 1. Subse-
quently, both the questions and guidelines are uti-
lized as the training, dev, and test set of the retrieval
model. However, the guidelines underwent a de-
duplication process based on string fuzzy matching
with a predetermined threshold of 0.75. Following
this procedure, the de-duplicated guidelines are in-
corporated into the guideline repository, resulting
in a final repository size of 33k.

5 Conclusion
We propose Guide-Align, a guideline-oriented
method to augment the safety and quality of LLMs.
We construct a comprehensive and detailed guide-
line library complemented by a retrieval model that
matches inputs with appropriate guidelines. These
elements constitute a plug-and-play module that
enables various LLMs to achieve alignment with
minimal expenditure. Experiments across diverse
datasets consistently illustrate that our methodol-
ogy bolsters model safety while preserving or en-
hancing performance in other dimensions. Further-
more, we curate an alignment dataset and employ
it to fine-tune a secure and dependable model, de-
noted as Labrador.

Limitations
Here, we discuss two limitations of our method:
Relying on a Safety-Trained LLM Our ap-
proach necessitates reliance on a robust, safety-
trained LLM in the initial phase to generate guide-
lines. Consequently, the quality of the guidelines
is contingent upon this model’s capabilities. Fur-
thermore, a diverse range of inputs is employed
to ensure the comprehensiveness of guidelines, al-
beit with associated cost implications. Therefore,
despite the desirability of using GPT-4, we have
chosen to employ GPT-3.5-turbo.
Constrained Cross-Linguistic Applicability
Our methodology involves employing a single
language retrieval model for extracting guidelines
from a library. However, considering that the input
may likely encompass multiple languages, we
recognize the necessity to establish a multilingual
guidelines library and train a cross-language
retrieval model in the future.
Broader Impact
Our research endeavors to enhance the safety and
practicality of models without compromising their
performance. Simultaneously, we aspire to encour-
age researchers to delve into the alignment of val-
ues concerning LLMs. The alignment dataset and
model we publish serve as a valuable resource, fos-
tering broader engagement within the research com-
munity and empowering researchers to explore and
advance the field of value alignment.
However, it is crucial to acknowledge and mit-
igate potential negative impacts associated with
our work. A notable concern is the risk of mis-
use, wherein, under the worst-case scenario, this
guide-based alignment approach could be altered to
a poisoning method based on malicious guidance.
This emphasizes the need for sustained vigilance
and ethical oversight throughout the development
and deployment of AI technologies.
Furthermore, the openness of the guideline li-
brary and alignment datasets introduces the pos-
sibility of reinforcing biases. Unforeseen biases
within the open-source guideline library or align-
ment datasets could inadvertently perpetuate un-
intended biases in AI systems. The presence of
biased information in these resources poses a sig-
nificant ethical challenge and underscores the ne-
cessity for continuous scrutiny, transparency, and
efforts to mitigate unintended consequences.
